record.paper_title: Massive Stars: Some Open Questions and the role of Multi-Object Spectroscopy
record.original_question: What is the correct effective-temperature scale of red supergiants, and how should stellar-atmosphere and evolutionary models be revised to reconcile the disagreement between temperatures inferred from TiO-band fitting and from spectral-energy-distribution and far-infrared methods? The paper identifies a persistent discrepancy between these two approaches and notes that it may arise because TiO bands form in upper atmospheric layers where opacity, structure, and three-dimensional effects are large. The related open issue is also whether the coolest effective temperatures reachable by red supergiants are strongly controlled by the adopted overshooting parameter in evolutionary models.

evidence.quote: However, Davies et al. (2013) fitting the Spectral Energy Distributions and using the Far Infrared Method obtain even higher temperatures than Massey et al. The discrepancy between both results can be attributed to the formation of TiO bands in upper layers, where opacity, structure and 3D effects are expected to be large.

Of course, this raises again a problem with the evolutionary models, although Davies et al. indicate that the position of the Teff limit in RSGs (i.e., the coolest Teff RSGs can reach) depends strongly on the adopted overshooting parameter and is thus very unceratin.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Red supergiants (RSGs) are evolved massive stars whose effective temperatures T_eff are commonly estimated by two largely independent observational techniques:

(i) fitting the strengths and shapes of TiO molecular absorption bands in the optical spectrum using model stellar atmospheres, and

(ii) fitting the broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) and/or applying the Far-Infrared Flux Method (FIFM), which rely on continuum fluxes formed in deeper atmospheric layers.

In practice these two approaches yield systematically different T_eff for the same RSGs, with TiO-based temperatures being several hundred Kelvin cooler than SED/FIFM-based temperatures. TiO bands form high in the atmosphere, where opacities, density/temperature stratification, and three-dimensional (convective/granulation) effects are expected to be large, while the continuum forms much deeper.

Problem. Determine the correct effective-temperature scale of red supergiants and provide a physically consistent revision of stellar-atmosphere and stellar-evolution models that simultaneously:

(a) reconciles the TiO-band temperatures with the SED and far-infrared continuum temperatures (specifying the role of upper-atmosphere opacity, non-LTE effects, hydrodynamic structure, and 3D granulation in the line-forming region of TiO);

(b) yields a quantitative prediction of the coolest T_eff a red supergiant can attain on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, and clarifies the dependence of this lower T_eff limit on the convective-overshooting parameter (and other mixing prescriptions) used in evolutionary tracks for massive stars.

Provide either a definitive unified T_eff scale calibrated against both diagnostics, or a rigorous demonstration of which atmospheric/evolutionary modelling assumptions must be modified to remove the discrepancy.
artifact.category_tag: Stellar astrophysics / red supergiant temperature scale
artifact.status_search_result: The discrepancy between TiO-band and SED/far-infrared temperature scales for red supergiants is well established and partially understood: 3D granulation and upper-atmosphere effects in the TiO line-forming region are widely identified as the dominant cause, and recent (2018, 2021, 2024) studies (e.g. LTE T_eff scales for Magellanic Cloud RSGs, line-depth-ratio diagnostics, and subsolar-metallicity RSG surveys) have refined and partially calibrated SED-based temperature scales and proposed empirical J−Ks color–temperature relations to bring TiO temperatures into agreement with evolutionary tracks. However, a fully consistent atmosphere+evolution model that resolves the discrepancy and pins down the coolest attainable T_eff (and its overshooting dependence) has not yet been agreed upon, so the question is best characterized as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: The Temperatures of Red Supergiants (Davies et al. 2013)
status_evidence.snippet: TiO-derived T_eff are systematically lower than SED/flux-integration values; 3D granulation in upper layers is the most likely cause of the discrepancy.
status_evidence.claim: Documents the TiO vs SED discrepancy and proposes 3D effects as the cause.

status_evidence.title: LTE effective temperature scale for red supergiants in the Magellanic Clouds (Tabernero et al. 2018)
status_evidence.snippet: Provides revised LTE T_eff scale for RSGs using high-resolution spectroscopy, partially reconciling diagnostics.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work has refined the RSG temperature scale.

status_evidence.title: Effective temperatures of red supergiants from line-depth ratios of Fe lines in the YJ bands (2021)
status_evidence.snippet: Independent NIR diagnostic provides T_eff consistent with SED-based scales, supporting partial resolution.
status_evidence.claim: Independent diagnostics support the higher (SED-like) T_eff scale.

status_evidence.title: Episodic mass loss in evolved massive stars II: RSGs at subsolar metallicity (A&A 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: Derives empirical J−Ks color–T_eff relations to bring TiO temperatures into agreement with evolutionary tracks; notes TiO discrepancy correlates with mass-loss rate.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2024) progress partially calibrates the TiO scale but the issue is not fully closed.
